title: Choose a doubling rule
observableEvidence: Explains a spelling choice using position or neighboring letters.
prompt: Compare three verbs. "plan" has one syllable and becomes "planned". "admit" is said ad-MIT, with the stress on its last syllable, and becomes "admitted". "visit" is said VIS-it, with the stress on its first syllable, and becomes "visited". Which explanation predicts the doubled t in "admitted" and fits all three examples?
solutionRepresentation: The stressed last syllable ends in one vowel and then one consonant, so that consonant doubles before -ed. Plan (one stressed syllable) and admit (stress on the last syllable) both double; visit (stress on the first syllable) does not, which rules out "every verb ending in t" and "every two-syllable verb". Doubling keeps the vowel before it short, so the long-vowel explanation is wrong.
solutionMethod: Test each explanation against every example, including the one that does not double.

deterministicValidator.canonicalAnswer: Best explanation: The stressed last syllable ends in one vowel then one consonant, so that consonant doubles before -ed.
acceptedAnswers: Best explanation: The stressed last syllable ends in one vowel then one consonant, so that consonant doubles before -ed.
deterministicValidator.equivalenceNotes: Structured choice field; the selected option must equal the correct option. No partial credit.

options.label: Every verb that ends in t doubles the t before -ed.
Every two-syllable verb doubles its last consonant before -ed.
The doubled letter makes the vowel before it long.
The stressed last syllable ends in one vowel then one consonant, so that consonant doubles before -ed.

hintSteps.prompt: One of the three verbs does not double its last letter. A good explanation has to account for that verb too.
hintSteps.question: Which verb keeps a single consonant before -ed?

hintSteps.prompt: Compare where the stress falls in the verbs that double and in the verb that does not.
hintSteps.question: What do the doubling verbs have in common that the other verb lacks?

hintSteps.prompt: Example with different verbs: "begin" (be-GIN) doubles its n before a vowel ending, but "open" (OH-pen) does not, because only begin is stressed on its last syllable.
hintSteps.question: Which explanation matches that pattern and all three verbs in this item?

accessibleAlternative: Three verbs: plan, one syllable, becomes planned. admit, said ad-mit with the stress on the last syllable, becomes admitted. visit, said vis-it with the stress on the first syllable, becomes visited. Choose the explanation that predicts the doubled t in admitted and fits all three verbs. Option 1: Every verb that ends in t doubles the t before -ed. Option 2: Every two-syllable verb doubles its last consonant before -ed. Option 3: The doubled letter makes the vowel before it long. Option 4: The stressed last syllable ends in one vowel then one consonant, so that consonant doubles before -ed.
